The deal was brokered by senior Shia political leaders. Esmail Qaani, commander of Iran's elite Quds Force, also arrived in Baghdad late on Monday to help defuse the situation.

data.author: Elis Gjevori

Saudi-backed forces defend strikes on Yemen's Hodeidah port
Saudi-backed forces have defended Saudi Arabia's latest attack on Yemen's civilian port of Hodeidah, with the number of casualties from today's strikes still unknown.
Salem al-Awalqi, the information minister in Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, told the government-run Saba news agency that the operation targeted facilities allegedly used by the Houthis to smuggle weapons into Yemen.
“The operation targeted specific components of the port facilities used to transport smuggled weapons, particularly ballistic missiles, from smuggling vessels,” he said, accusing the Houthis of dragging the port into the conflict.
“We reassure citizens that the flow of essential goods, humanitarian aid, and commercial activities will continue in accordance with established arrangements,” al-Awalqi claimed.
An earlier Saudi strike on the port on 17 November killed at least 15 people.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Palestinian and Israeli films present different shades of reality amid genocide
data.author: Joseph Fahim
data.summary:
Palestinian and Israeli films present different shades of reality amid genocide
Submitted by
Joseph Fahim
on
Fri, 11/20/2026 - 09:59
Hosam Abu Dan's Thirteen in Gaza and Ahmed Hassouna's Citizen Osama were filmed amid destruction
Thirteen in Gaza is an exploration of the moral rot that affects a society undergoing genocide (Toronto International Film Festival)
Off
A year after the so-called ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas in October 2025, Palestinian and Israeli cinemas have been scrambling to capture a volatile reality shaped by questions more complex than those that emerged in the immediate aftermath of 7 October.
Maintaining one’s dignity while surviving a sadistically dehumanising campaign targeting civilians was the central preoccupation of the handful of films about Gaza released between 2024 and early 2026.
The 2026 autumn season, however, offers a different set of inquiries: the deeply asymmetrical power dynamics between the Israeli aggressor and the Palestinians; the viability of what has now become the wistful dream of a two-state solution; the lingering ache for a lost, irretrievable homeland; and the newly exposed, unflattering realities of Gaza’s informal economy.
As the colossal success of NAZA has made evident, Gaza will continue to dominate cinema's narrative on Palestine for the foreseeable future.
Yet, as this fall's crop of films suggests, new dimensions will gradually come into focus as Palestinian filmmakers continue to grapple with uncertain terrain post-7 October.
Israeli cinema, meanwhile, will remain divided, caught between the pressure exerted by jingoist political leaders desperate to give their country a PR facelift and the competing impulse of leftist filmmakers seeking to restore the diminished international standing of a national cinema whose motivations can only be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Exclusive: UK doctors accused of antisemitism seek legal action against regulator over personal data leak
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
Exclusive: UK doctors accused of antisemitism seek legal action against regulator over personal data leak
Doctors in the UK who have been referred to the General Medical Council (GMC) for alleged antisemitism and Islamophobia are considering legal action after the regulator leaked sensitive data about them to The Times newspaper, Middle East Eye has learned.
The leak occurred following a Freedom of Information request submitted by the Times to the GMC, which asked for the number of doctors who had been complained about, investigated and sanctioned for antisemitism and Islamophobia since October 2023.
In its response, the GMC shared the reference numbers of 223 doctors, which allows them to be identified through the regulator’s public-facing database.
The GMC also included details of doctors’ ethnicities, which under UK law is a protected characteristic.
In a letter sent to doctors' groups this week, Claire Light, the GMC’s head of equality, diversity and inclusion, stated that internal data had been shared with The Times “in error”, and that the regulator had formally requested through their lawyers that the newspaper deletes the confidential data and does not disseminate it.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Fergie Chambers released in Spain as US admits court translation errors
data.author: Amandla Thomas-Johnson
data.summary:
Fergie Chambers released in Spain as US admits court translation errors
Submitted by
Amandla Thomas-Johnson
on
Fri, 11/20/2026 - 15:53
American pro-Palestinian activist is 'happy to breathe fresh air' following conditional release from prison as he fights US extradition request
Fergie Chambers outside Aranjuez prison following his release on Friday, 20 November 2026 (Reuters)
Off
Fergie Chambers, the American pro-Palestinian donor detained in Spain following a US extradition request, was granted provisional release on Friday after the Trump administration admitted to “substantial” translation errors in court documents submitted in support of its case.
Speaking outside Aranjuez prison on Friday following his release, Chambers described the charges against him as “baseless” and said he hoped his release was “the first step in a process of recognising that internationally”.
“I think this case is important for human rights, for people who want to speak out anywhere in the world,” he said.
The decision by the Criminal Chamber of Spain's National Court, known as the Audiencia Nacional, comes after Chambers had spent more than four months in custody since his arrest in Ibiza in July.
In its ruling, seen by Middle East Eye, the court said errors in the translation of documents submitted by US authorities had cast doubt on the reliability of the extradition request and weakened its basis.
The judges found that the development appeared to reduce the risk of Chambers fleeing and meant that his continued detention could no longer be justified.
His release is subject to several conditions, including weekly appearances before the court nearest his residence every Monday, surrendering his passport, a prohibition on leaving Spain and an obligation to appear before the court whenever summoned.
The court has also suspended its decision on whether to grant extradition while the translation issues are examined.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Cop31 draft agreement ‘the worst ever', campaigners warn
data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
Cop31 draft agreement ‘the worst ever', campaigners warn
Submitted by
Katherine Hearst
on
Fri, 11/20/2026 - 14:55
A second draft of the key text summarising the climate talks had references to a phase out of fossil fuels removed while centring carbon capture technologies
The Cop31 climate conference is being held at the Antalya Expo Centre in Turkey (AFP)
Off
Climate justice campaigners have hit out at the draft outcome of the global climate talks, describing it as the “worst” in the conference’s history.
The draft agreement, which outlines the key commitments of the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey, was stripped of all references to a phase-out of fossil fuels, but backed “accelerating carbon capture, utilisation and storage”, which civil society actors have derided as a “false solution” to climate breakdown.
“It's much weaker language across all fronts, and overall, when we look at it, it’s aggressive, it is backtracking, and it's not going to help developing countries," Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, told Middle East Eye.
"Rather, it is going to help the private sector, fossil fuel industry, and that is not what we came here for,” Singh said.
The “cover decision” is an overarching text which summarises the different negotiation outcomes, containing pledges intended to meet the goals of the Paris Agreement.
An initial draft which appeared on Monday was heavily edited, with many of the main commitments, including a transition away from fossil fuels and a $120bn target for finance to help developing countries adapt to the climate crisis, stripped out.
Crucially, the latest text substitutes a commitment to “transition away from fossil fuels” for a pledge to “irreversible global transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate resilience”.
The new draft also centres controversial carbon capture technologies, pledging to increase them 20- to 40-fold by 2035.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Houthis retaliate for coalition strikes with attack on Saudi power station and port
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Houthis retaliate for coalition strikes with attack on Saudi power station and port
Yemen’s Houthis said on Friday that they had attacked a power station in Saudi Arabia’s Al-Shuqaiq and the port of Jizan, in response to Saudi-led coalition strikes on Yemen.
“With God’s help, our armed forces carried out a precision military operation targeting the Al-Shuqaiq power station and the Port of Jizan. The strikes were accurate and direct, causing extensive damage,” Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on X.
Saree said the attack was a response to coalition strikes on the Saada and Mokha power stations, and on one of the quays at Hodeidah port earlier in the day.
“We assure the Saudi enemy that any attack on the Port of Hodeidah or power stations will be met with an immediate response targeting its ports and power stations,” he wrote.
On Friday, the coalition launched what it called a “special operation”, striking Hodeidah as well as targets in Sanaa, Saada and Taiz. The Houthis said strikes killed 41 people in the past 24 hours.

data.title: Middle East Eye: 'Iranians are after me': US Treasury secretary says he lives on a military base
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
'Iranians are after me': US Treasury secretary says he lives on a military base
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday that he was still living on a US military base after receiving unspecified threats from Iran, but vowed to keep squeezing the country economically.
"The Iranians are after me. I'm not going to be cowered by the Iranians. Life on the military base is good," Bessent said in an interview with CNBC.
"If the Iranians are after me, it means that they are being squeezed. We're going to continue squeezing them," he added.
The US Treasury has been tightening sanctions on Iran since the US and Israel launched strikes on the country in February.
"Operation Economic Outcast, which we are two and a half months into, is the greatest economic isolation of any country in history," Bessent said.
"For the first time in history since Iran started producing oil, they have no oil on the water, so there is no crude for anyone to buy. No Iranian crude for anyone to buy."

A tanker caught fire after a projectile struck it while sailing through the Strait of Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Friday.
The incident occurred 8 nautical miles north of the Omani town of Khasab, UKMTO said, adding that no casualties or environmental impact were reported.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Houthis say 41 killed as Saudi-led coalition launches 'special operation' in Yemen
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Houthis say 41 killed as Saudi-led coalition launches 'special operation' in Yemen
Saudi-led coalition strikes on Yemen killed 41 people in the past 24 hours, the Houthis said on Friday, after the coalition attacked the Red Sea port city of Hodeidah and other targets in what it called a “special operation”.
The coalition said it hit smuggling and weapons-transporting operations in Hodeidah while also carrying out attacks in Sanaa, Saada and Taiz governorates.
Meanwhile, Houthis had vowed to hit Jeddah and other Saudi Red Sea ports if Hodeidah was attacked, while warning airlines that Saudi airspace was “unsafe”. They also threatened Riyadh’s financial district and a power station in Al-Shuqaiq.
“We targeted operational capabilities at Hodeidah port that were used in smuggling operations and the transport of weapons and ballistic missiles,” Saudi coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki posted on X.
The coalition hit “military targets” in Sanaa, including missile and drone facilities and a supply depot, he added.
Two ballistic missiles were intercepted over the Jizan region near the Yemen border, he posted later, with debris falling in Al-Shuqaiq.
The Houthis’ Al-Masirah television broadcast images of a damaged power station in Mokha after a coalition air raid.

On the sidelines of the visit, Qatari Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani met his German counterpart Johann Wadephul.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Trump says US will find out about Iranian dirty bomb plot 'rumour'
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Trump says US will find out about Iranian dirty bomb plot 'rumour'
US President Donald Trump said on Friday that there was a "rumour" that Iran was building a dirty bomb. He added that if Iran was doing so, the United States would find out and stop it.
CNN had reported earlier this week that US intelligence indicated Iran could be attempting to build a dirty bomb and detonate it in Washington.
Iran's foreign ministry denied the allegations on Tuesday, calling them "baseless".
A dirty bomb is far less destructive than a nuclear bomb, which relies on a fission reaction.
Speaking to reporters, Trump also repeated his claim that the US has "total control" over the Strait of Hormuz.
"Last week, we took out record amounts of oil from the Hormuz Strait. Our navy has a blockade," he said. "We have total control over the Hormuz Strait."
"Iran will never have a nuclear weapon, ever," he added.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Shenzhen was not Yalta, but Europe was definitively sidelined
data.author: Marco Carnelos
data.summary:
Shenzhen was not Yalta, but Europe was definitively sidelined
Submitted by
Marco Carnelos
on
Fri, 11/20/2026 - 18:07
The US, China and Russia reached no substantive policy agreement, yet they sent a clear signal about where global power now resides
Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump pose for photos in Shenzhen, China, on 19 November 2026 (Vyacheslav Prokofyev/AFP)
Off
The first-ever US-Russia-China summit produced a thin declaration, and no carve-up of the world. But the format itself - three powers, one table, no Europeans - might matter more than anything they signed.
In February 1945, US President Franklin Roosevelt, UK Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Yalta to settle the shape of the postwar world.
Eight decades later, Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin sat down on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen for the first trilateral meeting ever held among the leaders of the US, China and Russia.
The comparison was irresistible. Yet after roughly 90 minutes of talks, what emerged was far more modest: a four-point joint “Declaration toward Peace”. The statement’s text suggests that what was supposed to be a historic event was mostly just a photo op.
This brings to mind another photograph, one that adorned the front page of The New York Times a quarter of a century ago, during a United Nations summit in New York in September 2000 that was meant to mark the beginning of a new era focused on “Millennium Development Goals”.
Instead of picturing the General Assembly Hall, the newspaper used an image of the leaders of the UN Security Council’s five permanent members around a table outside the summit - conveying to readers exactly who was really running the show.
Twenty-six years later, the number of leaders dropped from five to three; the two Europeans (the UK and France) were missing in action, and along with them, sadly, the entire EU.

data.title: Middle East Eye: US sanctions Iranian 'oil trustees' it accuses of evading sanctions
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
US sanctions Iranian 'oil trustees' it accuses of evading sanctions
The US Treasury on Friday imposed sanctions on four Iranians who served as "oil trustees".
It said they had sought to collect funds from illicit international oil sales and pass them to the Iranian government to evade earlier sanctions and a US naval blockade.
In many cases, the trustees kept the oil revenues for personal gain, the Treasury said in a statement.
Those sanctioned include Mohammad Javad Bavand, a former intelligence officer in Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and Majid Taj, brother of Mehdi Taj, the president of Iran’s football federation.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Palestinian man killed near Ramallah as Israeli raids sweep occupied West Bank
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Palestinian man killed near Ramallah as Israeli raids sweep occupied West Bank
A Palestinian man was killed by Israeli forces near Ramallah on Friday as the forces carried out raids, detentions and a home demolition across the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Hamza Masoud Salim Abdo, 42, was killed in Dura al-Qare, northeast of Ramallah, by Israeli forces who are still withholding his body, the Palestinian General Authority of Civil Affairs said.
In Jaba, south of Jenin, Israeli forces beat a man who was taken to hospital, the Palestinian Red Crescent said. A convoy of army vehicles later stormed the town and detained two young men. In nearby Qabatiya, soldiers fired on a vehicle and detained two people.
In Jericho, a young Palestinian man was shot in the foot during a raid on the al-Bayader neighbourhood.
South of Hebron, Israeli forces raided al-Fawwar refugee camp as residents left Friday prayers, firing tear gas and beating a young man who was later hospitalised.
In nearby Beit Ummar, Israeli forces stormed the town, ordered merchants to close their shops and fired barrages of tear gas and stun grenades, according to local media activist Mohammad Awad. He said soldiers severely beat and detained two men, aged 22 and 45.
In the Tulkarm governorate, several young men were detained as Israeli forces raided the town of Anabta.
Also on Friday, Israeli bulldozers demolished a home in al-Mazra’a al-Gharbiya, northwest of Ramallah.
Meanwhile, Israeli settlers stole the contents of a roadside fruit stand south of Jenin and trees from a nursery in Jaba, surveillance footage showed.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Vance refuses to endorse Iran strikes despite pressure from Trump
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Vance refuses to endorse Iran strikes despite pressure from Trump
US Vice President JD Vance on Friday declined to say whether he would have authorised strikes on Iran to stop it developing a nuclear weapon, sidestepping Trump’s calls for him to say the attacks were necessary and that he would carry them out again.
Speaking at a White House press conference alongside Trump, Vance said the decision to attack Iran in February had been the president’s call, “and my job is to support the president of the United States”.
After the midterm elections, Vance blamed the war for the Republicans’ historic losses and called for the US to exit the conflict.
His statement, posted on social media, was widely seen as a break with Trump as the vice president weighs a 2028 White House bid.
“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote. “The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay.”
Trump said on Friday that he was not unhappy with Vance’s conclusion but that it lacked a crucial element: an acknowledgement that the strikes were necessary and that Vance would make the same decision.
“People that work for me, they have a right to their opinion,” Trump said. “But I say, I know the Iranians, and, frankly, they’re crazy.”
Vice President JD Vance on Iran: "The goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we need to be doing. It's the biggest state sponsored terrorism. If they had a nuclear weapon, they would use it as leverage or God forbid they would attack and kill thousands, hundreds of thousands potentially, of innocent people. The president is the one who makes the decision and the president has said he would do it again. And my view is that my goal is and my job is to support the President of the United States."

data.title: Middle East Eye: Iran wants Trump to state explicitly he wants a deal, Araghchi says
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Iran wants Trump to state explicitly he wants a deal, Araghchi says
Iran still has hope that diplomacy can end its war with the United States, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said, adding that the two sides are still exchanging messages through mediators.
“We are seeking an agreement with the US that would ensure there is no further war afterwards,” Araghchi told an Iranian newspaper.
He said Tehran saw no need to change the intermediaries in the talks.
Before going any further, Iran wants guarantees that Washington is serious about negotiating, he said, and it has discussed the form and nature of possible confidence-building measures with the mediators.
Iran’s first demand is for US President Donald Trump to state explicitly that he wants an agreement, Araghchi said.
He added that it was not surprising for Trump to take a new position every day, or even to reverse what he had said the day before.
One of Iran’s red lines is that its enriched uranium must not leave the country, Araghchi stated, though he believed a fair solution could be reached.
He also said the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the US met Iran’s seven conditions.
His comments came hours after Trump reiterated that the US had "total control" over the strait.
Iran’s official position on the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons remains the same, and its nuclear doctrine has not changed, Araghchi added.

Sulaymaniyah is reeling from the economic toll of the Iran war and grappling with an emboldened regional power next door
A market in the city of Sulaymaniyah in Iraq's Kurdistan Region is said to be the largest bazaar in the region, on 11 November 2026 (Sean Mathews/MEE)
Off
If US President Donald Trump has his way, Baran* will be out of business.
The thirty-year-old Kurd is a trader who buys diesel in Iraq and sells it in Afghanistan. It’s a stressful gig, but one that can generate a tidy profit in a place like Iraqi Kurdistan. A truck laden with $20,000 worth of diesel in Iraq can sell in Kabul for around $24,000, leaving around $2,000 for the trader once expenses are paid. But it has to make it through Iran first.
“The journey is more dangerous now. It’s harder to find drivers. The border isn’t as reliable. The price of diesel has also shot up,” Baran, whose name has been changed to protect his identity, told Middle East Eye.
Trump says instead of restarting strikes on Iran, he wants to choke its economy. In addition to a naval blockade, the US is pressing countries like Turkey, Iraq and Pakistan to seal their borders with Iran. Earlier this month, the US announced a task force to blockade trade across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea.
Baran has no political beef with the US. On the contrary, he says, “George W. Bush overthrew Saddam Hussein. He helped Kurdistan. I don’t prefer Iran to the US,” he said over a glass of anise-flavoured Arak and hookahs at a restaurant in Sulaymaniyah.
“But this war has not been good for business or our economy.”
Baran is a microcosm of the city he calls home.
